3. The defendants entered appearance and contested the suit by filing a written statement and their case is that they took the loan of Tk. 18,00,000/- keeping the share certificates as pledge. There was a condition that those share certificates would be returned on the payment of the loan and in pursuance to the agreement the company regularly repaid the part of the loan upto 1971. After the liberation of Bangladesh the defendants wanted to repay the loan and to get back their share certificates which the bank failed to return back. Inspire of the returning the share certificates the bank was holding gross and charging interest and the money. Their further case is that claim of the bank is barred by limitation. 

 6. Mr. Imman Ali, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants in First Appeal No. 116 of 1987 submits that the company took the loan and the last repayment was made on 4.2.1971 and thereafter the company has not paid anything to the Bank. The learned Advocate contends that the present suit is barred under Article 57 of the Limitation Act as the bank has not instituted the suit within 3 (three) years from 04.2.1971 which is the date of last repayment by the company. He submits that on 18.3.1977 the bank wrote a letter to the company asking them to repay the loan to which they replied to on 29.3.1977 and in that letter they offered to repay the loan on condition of returning of the share certificates earlier kept with the bank. Without giving any reply and accepting the defendants offer the bank issued a legal notice on 13.3.1980 and thereafter instituted the present suit. The learned Advocate further contends that the bank has not written anything to the defendants-company nor the defendants company wrote anything to the bank within the period of limitation and as such the suit is barred under Section 19 of the Limitation Act. The learned Advocate contends that the last repayment was made on 29.3.77 but the company has not acknowledged to repay the loan, they simply offered that in case of the return of the share certificates the company may repay the outstanding dues which is very much a condition offered and when the plaintiff has not accepted the offer the same cannot be treated as a contract rather they have rejected the offer by issuing the legal notice. Mr. Imman Ali submits that the trial Court committed illegality in decreeing the suit as the claim of which is hopelessly barred by limitation. 

 7. Mr. Shaheed Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant in First Appeal No. 132 of 1987 submits that the company acknowledged the debt by their letter dated 29.3.77 and the suit was filed within the time prescribed by law and as such the suit is not barred by limitation. He further submits that when the company has accepted the bank's demand of the repayment of the loan the trial Court ought to have decreed the suit in full with up-to-date interest. 

 8. It is an admitted fact that the company took a loan of Tk. 15,00,000/- from the predecessor of the plaintiff-bank keeping the share certificates of Tk. 18,00,000/- as pledge with the bank and there was a condition that this pledged share certificates would be returned to the loanee after the full repayment of the loan and there was also a condition that the loanee would repay the loan within 4(four) years in quarterly instalments. It is also an admitted fact that the loanee repaied the one instalment on 4.2.71 and thereafter there was no repayment. It is well settled that a suit for recovery is governed by Article 57 of the Limitation Act which provides a period of three years for instituting a suit for recovery of any debt. Admittedly, the last repayment was made by the company on 4.2.1971. So, the limitation for bringing a suit for recovery of that will run from that date and from 4.2.1971 the last date was 4.2.1974 and the suit was not filed within that period. It appears from the record that the bank was sitting idle till 18.3.1977 when the issued a letter of that date marked Ext. 6 asking the defendants-company for the repayment of the loan and overdraft of outstanding. It appears from this letter that previously also on 12.3.75 the bank wrote a letter to the company on the repayment of the loan. It further appears that the loanee by Ext. 7 dated 29.3.77 in-formed the bank that over the matter of repayment there was previous discussion be-tween the parties and there was also a request for return of the share certificates to the loanee which were lying with the bank and in that letter the company agreed to repay the outstanding loan as on 1973 in return of the share certificates of Tk. 18,00,000/- lying with the bank. The bank it appears has not replied to that letter or accepted the contention of the loanee. Instead of that a legal notice marked Ext. 8 was issued on 13.3.1980 and they also at the same time filed the civil suit on 8.3.1980. 

 9. Mr. Shaheed Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-bank submits that by Ext. 7 the defendant company acknowledged the outstanding loan and agreed to repay the same and as such the limitation would run from that date. He submits that in view of the Ext. 7 the suit is not barred by limitation. The most valuable documents, that is, to be considered in this case is this letter Ext.7. 

 10. Mr. Inman Ali, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the loanee company submits' that this letter Ext. 7 cannot be construed as a promise on behalf of the company and this also not construed as acknowledgement of loan and undertaking to pay the same. He submits that even if it is construed to be an undertaking Section 25(3) of the Contract Act is a bar as this has been written long after the period of limitation as provided under Article 57 of the law of Limitation. In support of his submission Mr. Imman Ali placed reliance in the case of Seam Elenkatappayya Vs. Yalavarthi Venkatappayya, reported in A.I.R. (33) 1946 (Madras) 72, where it has been held that Section 25(3) was based on an agreement. As the plaintiff had refused the defendant's offer there was no agreement and hence the offer could not be made the basis of a claim under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act. lie further submits that even if Ext. 7 the construed as an acknowledgement in writing the plaintiff is not entitled to any benefit of it as the offer he was made after the period of limitation and in that view of the matter Section 19 of the Limitation Act has no manner of application. In support of his submission he placed reliance in the case of Shyam Sundar Misra Municipal Chair-man, Parlakimedi, reparted in A.I.R. 1964 Orissa 111, where it has been held that when the offer was made after the expiry of the period of limitation, Section 19 of the Limitation Act has no manner of application. He also placed reliance in the case of Ram Mangal Prasad Shahi Vs. Achhaibar Prasad Shahi and others, reported in A.I.R. 1954 (Patna) 575, where it has been held that the whole purpose of Section 19 of the Limitation Act is that, if there is an acknowledgement of liability before the suit to enforce that liability is barred, there will be fresh start of limitation and it does not a matter whether the acknowle4gement of liability is not addressed or communicated to the plaintiff or to one through whom he claims. It should be enough if there has been an acknowledgement of a liability within the meaning of Section 19 of the Limitation Act. He also placed reliance in the case of Bindle Dasya Chutiani Vs. Chota, reported in 16 C.W.N. 636, where it has been held that acknowledgement of a barred debt cannot give a fresh start to limitation in favour of the creditor. 

 11. Now the vital question before us is whether Ext. 7 can be construed as an acknowledgement or promise on the part of the loanee. Admittedly, the suit was filed on 8.3.1980 and the last payment was made by the loanee on 4.2.1971 and the bank demanded the repayment of their loan money on 8.3.1977 by Ext. 6 which is the first demand. The limitation in this case starts from 4.2.1971 and article 57 of the Limitation Act provides that the period of limitation in such a case is three years. So, even the bank's demand by Ext. 6 is beyond the specified period of limitation. It further appears that on receipt of this Ext. 6 the loanee company wrote Ext. 7 to the bank on 29.7.1977 which is the most vital document for both the sides. 

 12. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-bank submits that by this letter Ext. 7 the company has acknowldeged the debt and had agreed to repay the same and when they have not repaid the acknowledged amount as demanded by the bank the period of limitation is start from that date. Mr. Imman Ali, on the other hand submit that from a reading of Ext. 7 it would appear that this cannot be construed as an acknowledgement or a promise to repay the bank this is only a offer on certain conditions and that has not been accepted by the plaintiff-bank. He submits that when Ext. 6 as well as Ext. 7 have been issued after the period of limitation and when in Ext. 7 the company has not clearly acknowledged the debt and promise to repay the same this Ext. 7 cannot be used in construing the period of limitation. Relying on the aforesaid decisions he submits that such offers must have been made within the period of limitation. He argued that the period of limitation can be extended by an unconditional repay the loan which is very much absent in the present case. 

 14. From a consideration of these Exts. 6 and 7 and the other facts it appears to us that after the period of limitation Exts. 6 and 7 were issued and by Ext. 7 the period of limitation cannot be extended as that was a conditional offer. From the aforesaid decisions it appears that such offers must be within the period of limitation which has not been done in the present case before us. 

 15. Mr. Shaheed Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the bank placed before us a decision reported in 39 D.L.R. 243 (M/S. Daulat Ltd. Vs. Pubali Bank Ltd.) and submits that when the company has promised to pay a time barred debt in writing the period of limitation may be construed from the date of Ext. 7. That decision on the point given on the basis of a decision reported in 33 Indian Appeal 165 (Maniram Vs. Seth Rupchand), where it has been held that an unconditional acknowledgement has always been held to imply a promise to pay, because that is the natural inference if nothing is said to the contrary. But in the instant case Ext. 7 is undoubtedly a conditional offer of repayment of the outstanding debt and there was no unconditional offer to repay the time barred debt. In that view of the matter this decision has no manner of application in the present case before us. 

 16. Thus, after consideration of the materials on record and after hearing the learned Advocates of both the sides, we hold that the present suit is obliquely barred by limitation and the plaintiff is not entitled to any benefit of Exts. 6 and 7 which hive been initiated long after the period of limitation and that in Ext. 7 there was only a conditional offer which has not been acknowledged. The learned Subordinate Judge has committed an error and wrong in passing the decree. 

 17. Having given our anxious consideration to the materials on record and the relevant laws, we hold that the decree has been passed wrongly and the plaintiff is not entitled to any decree as he claimed is barred by limitation. So, this is a fit case where this Court should interfere and set aside the decree.
